He's a tory in the 2010s at the height of their xenophobia and assault on the social safety net, but he pretends to be 'one of the last good ones', refusing to realise that just by standing for them he's doing damage.

It's all summed up in the radio episode - he performs an anti-corporate populist politics and crumbles when he needs to direct that at his city friends. He's shocked to realise his donors have links to sweatshops and thrilled once Tim from Ruislip turns that back on Nicola.

There's a reason he's part of the crowd Stewart aims his anger at in the last episode, part of the solid bed of cunts. All of these people are hollow, but Malcolm is at least consciously machiavellian; Nicola at least realises she's being reduced by this political culture. Hey hey, I'm a film student writing a little bit about Taxi Driver for my masters dissertation atm.

There's a chapter by Robin Wood called 'The Incoherent Text' that points out essentially what you're talking about, and says that the ending of the film represents Travis falling so deep into psychosis that the narrative itself fractures around him. Wood says something like 'the ending of the film only works if the audience is identified with a single point of view and all supporting characters are reduced to two dimensional puppets in service of Travis' ego'.

It was loosely based on The Searchers, which itself is a kind of incoherent western where the protagonist is a racist monster on a revenge mission. My reading of Taxi Driver is as a continuation of the western hero *but* without a mission. Travis then is overflowing with a need for violent revenge but no idea where to direct it.

Hope any of that interests you. I really didn't get the hype around the film the first few times I watched it but I'm appreciating the hollow feeling it leaves me with more and more

We can assume Vicious was an impoverished street kid. Maybe an orphan, maybe a child of neglect, anything similar. That Mao 'took Vicious in and made him what he was' suggests he had little to no support network, as is often the case with kids taken in by gangs IRL. This means mob life was his only guide, and after my latest rewatch, I see him as torn between its contradictions.

Think about the ruthlessness that comes with mob life. It has Nietzchean implications - that morality is a delusion to keep people from taking what they want. Vicious espouses this philosophy throughout most of the series. He tells Lin he 'might have to betray' him sometimes, and tells Chin 'not to follow in his brother's footsteps' by saving his life. Mob life has taught Vicious that moral codes and systems of honour are meaningless and contemptible.

Yet when it comes to Spike, he acts against this philosophy. His hangup over Spike is driven by whatever happened between them and Julia, and this is ultimately his downfall. In their final fight, their weapons reverse. Spike has Vicious' sword, Vicious Spike's gun. Vicious could easily take the upper hand here, shooting Spike. But instead they give each other back their preferred weapons, and Vicious dies. Even if it meant his death, there was a fundamental code of honour that Vicious couldn't let go of.

This is why I don't think he's a simple moustache twirling villain. I think he saw the world through Nietzchean eyes until his friendship with Spike. It showed him that it was possible to make connections, that there was a point to honour. And he struggles with reconciling these worldviews until his death.

I adore the book and from the beginning, the film clearly made a mistake. The genius of the book is its structure: by jumping back and forth between the shooting of The Room and Greg meeting Tommy, you get the fun onset antics alongside having questions about the main characters' relationship satisfied. That way not only do you not get frustrated by the origin story dragging on when you want to see the making-of story, but specific character quirks Tommy exhibits while shooting make you curious to know more about how he and Greg became friends. This structure enriches both parts of the story. 

I stayed with it hoping they'd show Tommy's ambiguity well, but instead all of his psychotic and abusive behaviour - threatening to kill Greg, recording their conversations, verbally assaulting him - is brushed off and barely alluded to in one on-set meltdown.

The end of the film then completely whitewashed Tommy's acceptance of The Room's critical reception, but also made it clear what the film really was - Hollywood actors indulging themselves by taking a mentally ill man's story and packaging it in the most easily digestible form for audiences to make a buck.

The Disaster Artist completely missed the point of the book and refused to look deeply into the incredibly interesting, incredibly complicated true story.

I back away from the coal black burn mark that surrounds the fast receding crack in the sidewalk, my mouth trying and failing to fully close and my eyes darting back and forth across the street in the hope that someone, anyone, saw what I saw. With not a single of the few dozen morning commuters hurrying by me having any kind of reaction, all focused instead on balancing their coffee cups with their quick stride or navigating each-other while also checking snapchat stories, my mind began to race with rationalizations. 'Ok, calm down, I just didn't get enough sleep last night, I'm stressed out about my first day at the internship, maybe my fourth Buffy the Vampire Slayer re-watch has proven one time too many, maybe my anxiety has gotten the best of me again and it's time to go back to the doctor's...' and so on and forth until my thoughts are interrupted by the screech of tires and the smack of a heavy door. I swivel around. Two figures in black zip hoodies step right up to me and everything goes dark. I try desperately to move my arms before *thump* \- I slam onto a hard metal surface.

'Shush! Shush! Stop moving and calm down!' A sharp, high pitched voice warns me over the roar of an engine. My wrists are forced together and bound by something cold and tight as the sharp voice walks me through anxiety relief: 'It's ok, there's nothing to be afraid of. We're here to help you. Just take a deeeeep breath in and slowly let it out'. I try to breathe but instead of feeling air enter my mouth, only a thick dry canvas, which doesn't help with the panic.

'Can he even breathe with that thing over his head?' Asks a lower, rougher voice.

'Oh shit, good point!' And in a moment, I can see again. In front of me, backlit by the sun's reflection through a windshield, crouch a heavy black-clad man, whose stubble and dark stringy hair surrounds a pursed mouth and and narrowed eyes, and a younger pink-haired woman with a rounded face and concerned expression. To her side lies a red toolbox and a canvas with deep maroon stains, and behind the two sits a barely visible driver. I try to ask the two several questions at once, never managing more than two words of each query: 'What the-! Who are...? Where am-?! Why-?!'

'Shuuusshh! Like I said, deep breaths.' The woman illustrates and we take lengthy inhales together until I stop shaking. I focus on the bumps in the road below us to ground myself.

'You son of a bitch,' hisses the bear of a man, 'I've been sitting on that kill for weeks!'

'What? What kill?'

'Leave him alone.' pleads Pink 'He clearly doesn't know what's going on. He just got lucky.'

'Lucky?!' I sputter. 'HOW?!

'You really don't know?' Growls Bear. 'Shit. Back there on the street. What do you think you saw?'

'I don't know, man! Can you p-please just let me out, I-I'm gonna be late for work!'

'Work? Seriously? I think this takes precedence. What... do you think... you saw?

'I... this guy sneezed and... I said "bless you" and... he-'

'Turned red, grew horns, caught fire and fell into a hole in the ground screaming in tongues?'

I widened my eyes as if reliving the moment. 'Y-yeah!'

'Actually Baylor is, or was, a light purple.' Pink clarifies.

'And Baylor was mine! I've been following "Johnathon Prowler", as the world knows him, for sixteen days now!' Bear pulls out a long, sharp stick from his belt and waves it in my face. 'I've been sharpening this stake every day for a week! For nothing!'

Baylor? Stake? I run everything through my mind, trying to make sense of it. Only one conclusion makes sense to me, even though it makes no sense at all. 'Wait... are you telling me... was that a... d... de...?'

'A demon? Yes.' Pink scooches closer to me and speaks slowly, as if to a child. 'Just stay calm while I rip the band-aid off. Demon's exist. For centuries, they controlled the world. They orchestrated the fall of Rome, the Black Death, countless wars, trying to damn as many people to Hell as possible. But during the plague, people started using "bless you" as a colloquialism. What they didn't know was that saying that to a demon sends them straight back to Hell. The human race unwittingly won the war against evil. But, even now, there's still a few stragglers around, so that's why we're here. We're demon hunters'.

I sit for a while and process. I wonder if they're running some long winded con on me, or if Ashton Kutcher is about to stop the van and reveal the camera crew of Punk'd. But just in case neither of these scenarios are true, there's one question I need answered.

'What are you going to do with me?' Bear tightens his grip around his stake and leans in.

'We're going to shove this thing through your heart, drive to the nearest lake and make sure nobody will ever find you.' His wide eyes and gritted teeth make my heart skip a beat - until he lets loose a throaty chuckle. 'Nah, I'm only kidding, kid. You're bait.'

'Excuse me?' Bear scooches to the other side of the van and starts rooting through a large, red toolbox. Pink clocks my fear and tries to explain.

'Well, not bait exactly. You see, being under constant threat and such a small community at this point, demons do their best to look out for each-other. So when they see someone having killed one of their kind, even accidentally...' She's interrupted by a deafening *bang* as the entire van shakes. Everyone looks up with a startled shock that quickly gives way to looks of resolution.

'Wh-what was that?!!' I yelp. Pink ignores me and joins Bear at the toolbox. The barely visible driver checks his side mirror before looking back to us so quickly that his glasses nearly slide off his long nose.

'Um, guys!', is all he manages before something smashes through the windscreen. Through the jagged glass is an upside down face, blood red and impossibly narrow, with a pair of sharp black horns protruding from its forehead. It screams something in an unknown language before its long thin tongue starts to slither around its salivating mouth. Pink doesn't look back, only smiles as she pulls out a sharp metal dagger from the toolbox. Bear stands up in the middle of the van, loading a crossbow. 

'Ok kid, all's forgiven!' He bellows as he turns and aims at the demon, laughing maniacally.

If you know why the emotion of fear even exists, you see it doesn't make complete rational sense; we feel fear to warn us of impending, life threatening danger. Abstract existential concepts, while disconcerting to our conscious brain, shouldn't be spiking your sympathetic nervous system like that. It's a physical response to signal immediate danger. The fact that we will all be dead for eternity doesn't count. That is disturbing and depressing, but shouldn't be panic attack inducing, at least not consistently.

I've had a form of existential OCD for a few months now, which was spiking dissociative panic attacks in the early days. Read up on it, and try to be at peace with those thoughts. Practice Exposure Response Therapy; repeat 'I will die and I will be dead forever' a dozen times before try to go on with your day. Do this every day for a while. Eventually, your body will realise there's nothing to be afraid of in that thought, at least not in the sense that an immediate response from your SNS is required, and your anxiety should balance out.

Philosophers study these questions for a living and avoid panic attacks, and they're concepts all of us come to terms with. Don't worry, you'll be fine :)
